title: PhD in Switzerland: CHF 50,000-68,000 Salaries and What They Actually Buy
seoTitle: PhD Switzerland Salary: CHF Scales, Costs & How to Apply
seoDescription: Swiss PhD salaries run CHF 50,000-68,000 (SNSF floor CHF 50,000 from 2026; ETH postdocs CHF 90k+). Salary scales, living costs, and how admission works.
intro: Switzerland pays the world’s highest doctoral salaries — CHF 50,000-68,000 on contracts with annual raises. What the scales look like and what they buy.
description: PhD in Switzerland: salary scales by institution, living costs, admission routes and who the system fits.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Swiss PhD salaries: CHF 50,000-68,000 on contract scales — and what they buy in Zurich, Basel and Lausanne.
content:
Switzerland pays doctoral researchers more than any other country — and unlike its stipend-based neighbours, it does so through employment contracts with annual raises, pension contributions and social insurance. A Swiss PhD is a job in one of the world’s richest labour markets, and the salary is only the headline: what the package buys, how the scales rise, and what the country asks in return (rents, notably) is the real story.

What doctoral researchers earn

Institution typeTypical doctoral salaryExamples
ETH Domain (ETH Zurich, EPFL, PSI, Empa, WSL, Eawag)CHF 50,000-68,000/year, rising annuallyETH Zurich doctoral positions
Cantonal universities (UZH, Basel, Bern, Geneva)CHF 42,000-58,000/yearUZH, University of Basel doctoral contracts
SNSF-funded projectsMinimum CHF 50,000 (from 2026)Swiss National Science Foundation project PhDs
Applied universities (Fachhochschulen)CHF 45,000-58,000/yearZHAW, HES-SO doctoral places

Two anchors frame the numbers. The Swiss National Science Foundation set a doctoral minimum of CHF 50,000 a year from 2026 for its funded projects — the country’s salary floor for research. At the top, ETH Zurich and EPFL doctoral positions run well above that, and postdoctoral salaries at the ETH Domain reach CHF 90,000-94,000 in the first year. Salaries step up with each year of the doctorate, so the four-year sum outpaces the entry figure by a wide margin.

[[chart:swiss-phd-salary]]

Net of Swiss tax and social contributions, expect roughly CHF 3,700-4,900 a month depending on canton and stage — our net-pay comparison puts Switzerland’s take-home at nearly double the European doctoral average.

What the salary meets: Swiss costs

Zurich rooms run CHF 900-1,400 a month; Geneva and Basel sit close behind; Bern, Lausanne and the smaller university towns (Fribourg, Neuchâtel, Lugano) price 15-30 per cent lower. Health insurance — mandatory, bought privately — costs CHF 250-450 a month and is the budget line newcomers always underestimate. The net result: a single doctoral researcher lives comfortably in every Swiss city, a couple on one salary lives carefully, and the family arithmetic improves sharply once a partner’s work rights kick in — Swiss family permits carry full labour-market access.

How to get in

Swiss doctoral admission is supervisor-driven: positions are advertised on university portals and Euraxess, but many ETH and EPFL doctorates begin with a direct application to a professor — CV, transcript, and a statement that maps your methods onto their current projects. Our supervisor email templates transfer directly. English is the working language of Swiss research almost everywhere; no certificate is typically demanded beyond interview-level fluency, though some cantonal universities list B2-C1 for certain programmes.

Two funding variants matter alongside employment: the Swiss Government Excellence Scholarship, which funds a 6-12 month research stay with the supervisor’s prior acceptance (CHF 2,450 a month), and foundation grants for specific nationalities. Both are best treated as entry ramps to the salaried system rather than alternatives to it.

Who Switzerland fits

  • Savers and supporters: the only European system where a doctoral salary supports remittances or a family comfortably.
  • STEM and quantitative researchers: the ETH Domain’s scale is unmatched — robotics, quantum, climate, biotech.
  • Long-game applicants: Swiss PhD-to-postdoc-to-industry pipelines (pharma, precision engineering, finance) are the strongest retention system in Europe.

The honest counterweights: Swiss admission is supervisor-driven and competitive, housing in Zurich and Geneva demands early action, and mandatory health insurance bites a real CHF 250-450 from every month. Applicants who would find the Nordics’ work-life culture more congenial, or Germany’s tuition-free breadth more forgiving, should let those preferences count — Switzerland wins on money so decisively that the other columns deserve a deliberate look rather than a default. Where money is the column that matters most, nothing else in Europe competes.
